Work in $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}:=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda$, the
$\mathbb Q$-scalar extension of the stable graded ring
([[def-stable-graded-ring-of-symmetric-functions]]). Its power sums
$p_1,p_2,\dots$ ([[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]])
are algebraically independent generators:
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q[p_1,p_2,\dots]$, and for every $d$ the products
$p_\lambda$, $\lambda\vdash d$, form a $\mathbb Q$-basis of
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^d$
([[prop-power-sums-form-a-rational-not-integral-stable-basis]]).

A **specialization** is a $\mathbb Q$-algebra homomorphism
$f\mapsto f[A]$ from $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}$ to a commutative
$\mathbb Q$-algebra. By the algebraic independence of the power sums, a
specialization is determined by the sequence of values $\bigl(p_k[A]\bigr)_{k\ge1}$,
and conversely every sequence of elements of a commutative $\mathbb Q$-algebra
extends uniquely to a specialization. For specializations $A,B$, a scalar
$c\in\mathbb Q$ and a one-letter alphabet $t$ one defines the specializations
$A+B$, $-A$, $AB$, $c\cdot A$ and $tA$ by their power-sum values

$$p_k[A+B]:=p_k[A]+p_k[B],\qquad p_k[-A]:=-p_k[A],\qquad p_k[AB]:=p_k[A]\,p_k[B],$$

$$p_k[c\cdot A]:=c\,p_k[A],\qquad p_k[t]:=t^k\ \ \text{and hence}\ \ p_k[tA]=t^k p_k[A].$$

Here $c\cdot A$ is a coefficient multiplicity, to be distinguished from the
one-letter alphabet $t$, for which $p_k[t]=t^k$ is a power and
$p_k[tA]=t^k p_k[A]$; all occurrences of $tX$, $t^{-1}$, $tA$ and
$\sigma[t]$ on this page use this one-letter convention. The symbol $1$
denotes the one-letter alphabet with $p_k[1]=1$ for all $k$, and $-1$ denotes
its plethystic negative with $p_k[-1]=-1$ for all $k$
([[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]]); it is
**not** the ordinary one-letter alphabet whose letter is minus one, for which
$p_k$ would equal $(-1)^k$. One writes $f[A+B]$, $f[-A]$, $f[AB]$ and
$f[c\cdot A]$ for the images of $f$ under these specializations.

Define $X^{\perp}$ to be the specialization with $f[X^{\perp}]:=f^{\perp}$ for
all $f$, where $f^{\perp}$ is the adjoint of multiplication by $f$ with respect
to the Hall inner product $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_H$
([[def-hall-inner-product-on-symmetric-functions]]), characterized by
$\langle f^{\perp}g,h\rangle_H=\langle g,fh\rangle_H$. It exists and is unique
because the Hall form is nondegenerate on each finite-dimensional graded piece
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^d$; the adjoints of commuting multiplication operators
commute, so the operators $f^{\perp}$ span a commutative
$\mathbb Q$-algebra and $X^{\perp}$ is a specialization in the sense above.

Define the series
$$\sigma[X]:=\sum_{n\ge0}h_n[X],$$
$h_n$ the complete homogeneous symmetric function
([[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]]).
Here $\sigma$ is interpreted in the graded completion of $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}$
(or with a formal degree variable): it is a formal series, not an element of
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}$, and every occurrence of $\sigma$ below is to be read
degree by degree. Every Hall pairing of a series with a polynomial is the
finite sum obtained by truncating to the degrees of the polynomial. No
convergence of a scalar infinite sum is asserted, and no value of $\sigma$ at
a specialization with infinitely many letters is interpreted analytically.

For $r\ge1$, let $p_r\in\Lambda^r$ be the compatible sequence of finite
power-sum polynomials $p_r(x_1,\ldots,x_N)=\sum_{i=1}^N x_i^r$
([[def-stable-graded-ring-of-symmetric-functions]],
[[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]]). For a
partition $\lambda$, set $p_\lambda:=\prod_i p_{\lambda_i}$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Write
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}:=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda$ and
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^d:=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda^d$. Then
$$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q[p_1,p_2,\ldots],$$
and for every $d\ge0$, the family $\{p_\lambda:\lambda\vdash d\}$ is a
$\mathbb Q$-basis of $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^d$. These families are not in
general $\mathbb Z$-bases of $\Lambda^d$: in degree two,
$h_2=\tfrac12(p_{(1,1)}+p_{(2)})$ has nonintegral coordinates in the power-sum
basis.

Work in $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda$. For a
partition $\rho$ write
$m_i(\rho):=\#\{j:\rho_j=i\}$ and
$z_\rho:=\prod_{i\ge1}i^{m_i(\rho)}m_i(\rho)!$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]]).

For partitions $\lambda$ and $\rho$ of the same integer, let $N(\lambda,\rho)$
be the number of ways to distribute the cycles of a permutation $w$ of cycle
type $\rho$ among the $\ell(\lambda)$ rows, labelled $1,\dots,\ell(\lambda)$,
so that row $j$ receives cycles whose lengths sum to $\lambda_j$. Cycles of
equal length count as **distinct** here, because they are distinct cycles of
$w$; equivalently,

$$N(\lambda,\rho)=\sum_{(m_i^{(j)})}\ \prod_{i\ge1}\frac{m_i(\rho)!}{\prod_j m_i^{(j)}!},$$

the sum over all matrices $(m_i^{(j)})$ of nonnegative integers with
$\sum_j m_i^{(j)}=m_i(\rho)$ for every $i$ and
$\sum_i i\,m_i^{(j)}=\lambda_j$ for every $j$; each summand is the product
over $i$ of the number of ways to assign the $m_i(\rho)$ labelled cycles of
length $i$ to rows with the prescribed multiplicities $m_i^{(j)}$, so
$N(\lambda,\rho)$ is a nonnegative integer. Then

$$h_\lambda=\sum_{\rho\vdash|\lambda|}N(\lambda,\rho)\,\frac{p_\rho}{z_\rho}\qquad\text{in }\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}.$$

In particular $h_d=\sum_{\rho\vdash d}p_\rho/z_\rho$ for every $d\ge0$.

For $k\ge1$, the **$k$-th power-sum symmetric polynomial** is

$$p_k:=x_1^k+\cdots+x_n^k.$$

For $k\ge0$, the **$k$-th complete homogeneous symmetric polynomial** is

$$h_k:=\sum_{a_1+\cdots+a_n=k}x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_n^{a_n}.$$

Thus $h_0=1$, while for $n=0$ one has $h_k=0$ when $k>0$. Both families are fixed by every permutation of the variables.

Put $e_0=1$ and $e_k=0$ for $k>n$. For every $k\ge1$,

$$k e_k=\sum_{i=1}^k(-1)^{i-1}e_{k-i}p_i.$$

In particular, for $k\le n$ this recursively relates $e_k$ to $p_1,\ldots,p_k$, while for $k>n$ it gives

$$p_k-e_1p_{k-1}+\cdots+(-1)^ne_np_{k-n}=0.$$

No division is used, so the identities hold over every commutative ring.

For every commutative ring $R$ and every $n\in\mathbb N$, substitution $T_k\mapsto e_k$ is an $R$-algebra isomorphism

$$R[T_1,\ldots,T_n]\longrightarrow R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]^{\operatorname{Sym}_n}.$$

Equivalently, every symmetric polynomial has a unique expression $Q(e_1,\ldots,e_n)$.

Let $\Lambda(x)$ and $\Lambda(y)$ be two copies of the graded ring
[[def-stable-graded-ring-of-symmetric-functions]], with degree pieces
$\Lambda^a(x)$ and $\Lambda^b(y)$. Define the **bidegree-completed tensor
product** by
$$\Lambda(x)\widehat\otimes\Lambda(y):=\prod_{a,b\ge0}\bigl(\Lambda^a(x)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda^b(y)\bigr).$$

Addition is componentwise. If $u=(u_{a,b})$ and $v=(v_{a,b})$, their product
has component
$$ (uv)_{a,b}:=\sum_{i=0}^{a}\sum_{j=0}^{b}u_{i,j}v_{a-i,b-j},$$
where multiplication in each tensor factor is the graded multiplication of
$\Lambda$. This is a finite sum for each fixed $(a,b)$, so it defines a
commutative ring; the unit has component $1\otimes1$ at $(0,0)$ and zero
elsewhere.

The **Cauchy kernel** is the element
$$\Omega(x,y):=\prod_{r,s\ge1}(1-x_r y_s)^{-1}$$
interpreted bidegree by bidegree: its degree-$(d,d)$ component is the stable
degree-$d$ coefficient of the finite products, and all components $(a,b)$ with
$a\ne b$ are zero. Thus $\Omega$ belongs to the diagonal bidegrees of this
completion, not to the finite-support graded ring $\Lambda$ itself.

Let $\Omega(x,y)$ be the Cauchy kernel in the bidegree completion
[[def-bidegree-completed-symmetric-function-tensor-product]]. In
$\Lambda(x)\widehat\otimes\Lambda(y)$,
$$\Omega(x,y)=\sum_\lambda h_\lambda(x)m_\lambda(y)=\sum_\lambda s_\lambda(x)s_\lambda(y).$$
In the componentwise rational completion
$$\prod_{a,b\ge0}\bigl(\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^a(x)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^b(y)\bigr),$$
it also has the expansion
$$\Omega(x,y)=\sum_\lambda z_\lambda^{-1}p_\lambda(x)p_\lambda(y),\qquad z_\lambda:=\prod_{r\ge1}r^{m_r(\lambda)}m_r(\lambda)!,\qquad m_r(\lambda):=\#\{i:\lambda_i=r\}.$$
All three sums are by bidegree $(d,d)$; the empty products indexed by
$\varnothing$ equal $1$.

For every $d\ge0$, the stable Schur functions $\{s_\lambda:\lambda\vdash d\}$
form a $\mathbb Z$-basis of $\Lambda^d$ and are orthonormal for the Hall form:
$$\langle s_\lambda,s_\mu\rangle_H=\delta_{\lambda\mu}$$
for all partitions $\lambda,\mu$.

The **Hall inner product** is the graded $\mathbb Z$-bilinear form on the
stable ring $\Lambda$ ([[def-stable-graded-ring-of-symmetric-functions]])
characterized by
$$\langle h_\lambda,m_\mu\rangle_H=\delta_{\lambda\mu}$$
for all partitions $\lambda,\mu$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[thm-elementary-and-complete-families-freely-generate-the-stable-ring]],
[[thm-monomial-symmetric-functions-form-the-integral-stable-basis]]), where
$\delta_{\lambda\mu}=1$ if $\lambda=\mu$ and $0$ otherwise. In particular,
homogeneous components of unequal degrees are orthogonal.
For the empty partition, $h_\varnothing=m_\varnothing=1$, so
$\langle1,1\rangle_H=1$.

For each $d\ge0$, the proven integral bases give unique finite expansions
$$f_d=\sum_{\lambda\vdash d}a_\lambda h_\lambda,\qquad g_d=\sum_{\mu\vdash d}b_\mu m_\mu$$
for $f_d,g_d\in\Lambda^d$. Define their degree-$d$ pairing by
$$\langle f_d,g_d\rangle_H:=\sum_{\lambda,\mu\vdash d}a_\lambda b_\mu\delta_{\lambda\mu}.$$
For $f=\sum_d f_d$ and $g=\sum_d g_d$ in the algebraic direct sum $\Lambda$,
set $$\langle f,g\rangle_H:=\sum_d\langle f_d,g_d\rangle_H.$$
Only finitely many $d$ contribute because $f$ and $g$ have finite degree
support. The unique expansions in the two integral bases make this a
well-defined $\mathbb Z$-bilinear form; the displayed basis rule determines it
uniquely on all of $\Lambda$.

Extend the Hall form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_H$ on $\Lambda$
$\mathbb Q$-bilinearly to
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}:=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda$. For partitions
$\lambda$ and $\mu$, let
$$z_\lambda:=\prod_{r\ge1}r^{m_r(\lambda)}m_r(\lambda)!,\qquad m_r(\lambda):=\#\{i:\lambda_i=r\}.$$
Then
$$\langle p_\lambda,p_\mu\rangle_H=\delta_{\lambda\mu}z_\lambda.$$
In particular, power sums of unequal degrees are orthogonal.

Fix an integer $n\ge0$ and work over $\mathbb C$. Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be
partitions of $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]), and let
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ be the tensor product of their complex
Specht modules, a finite-dimensional complex $S_n$-module
([[def-tensor-product-of-complex-representations]],
[[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]). The
**Kronecker coefficient** $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ of a third partition
$\nu\vdash n$ is the multiplicity of $S^\nu$ in this tensor product:

$$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu):=\frac{\dim_{\mathbb C}\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}}{\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu},$$

where $\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}$ is the isotypic
component of type $S^\nu$
([[def-isotypic-component-of-a-completely-reducible-representation]]).

**Well-definedness.** The module $S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ is
finite-dimensional, and $\operatorname{char}\mathbb C=0$ does not divide the
order of the finite group $S_n$, so complex Maschke's theorem gives complete
reducibility
([[thm-maschkes-theorem-for-finite-groups-over-fields-whose-characteristic-does-not-divide-the-group-order]],
[[cor-finite-dimensional-representations-are-completely-reducible-when-char-k-does-not-divide-group-order]],
[[def-completely-reducible-representation]]). The complex Specht modules
$S^\nu$, $\nu\vdash n$, are a complete list of pairwise inequivalent
irreducible $S_n$-modules
([[thm-complex-specht-modules-are-irreducible]],
[[thm-complex-irreducibles-of-symmetric-groups-are-specht-modules]],
[[cor-distinct-specht-modules-are-inequivalent]]). Consequently a decomposition
into irreducibles has the form
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\cong\bigoplus_{\nu\vdash n}m_\nu S^\nu$
with nonnegative integer multiplicities $m_\nu$, and the isotypic component of
type $S^\nu$ is the direct sum of exactly the $m_\nu$ copies of $S^\nu$
appearing in any such decomposition; in particular
$\dim_{\mathbb C}(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu)_{(S^\nu)}=m_\nu\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu$
and $\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu>0$ because $S^\nu$ is irreducible. Hence
$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=m_\nu$ is a nonnegative integer, independent of the chosen
decomposition, and $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ is by definition the multiplicity of
$S^\nu$ in $S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$.

**The internal product.** For partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ call
$$(\lambda,\mu)\longmapsto S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$$
the **internal (Kronecker) product** of the $S_n$-representations $S^\lambda$
and $S^\mu$. Unlike the outer induction product
$\operatorname{Ind}_{S_a\times S_b}^{S_{a+b}}(S^\alpha\boxtimes S^\beta)$ of
[[thm-outer-littlewood-richardson-rule]], which takes a pair of modules of
degrees $a$ and $b$ to a module of degree $a+b$, the internal product keeps the
rank: both inputs and the output are $S_n$-modules of the same degree $n$. The
two operations are different constructions on different data; the outer product
is mentioned here only for contrast and is not used in this definition.

No form of the Axiom of Choice is used: the tensor product, Maschke's theorem,
the Specht classification and the isotypic decomposition are finite-dimensional
complex representation theory of a finite group.

Let $\operatorname{ch}:R_S\to\Lambda$ be the Frobenius characteristic restricted
to the graded ordinary representation ring of the symmetric groups
([[def-frobenius-characteristic-map]],
[[def-graded-ordinary-representation-ring-of-symmetric-groups]]). By
[[thm-frobenius-characteristic-is-an-isometric-graded-ring-isomorphism]] it is a
degree-preserving $\mathbb Z$-module isomorphism onto the stable symmetric
function ring $\Lambda=\bigoplus_{m\ge0}\Lambda^m$, so its restriction
$\operatorname{ch}:R(S_m)\to\Lambda^m$ is an isomorphism for every $m\ge0$.

For $f\in\Lambda^m$ and $g\in\Lambda^n$ define
$$f*g:=\begin{cases}\operatorname{ch}\bigl(\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(f)\cdot\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(g)\bigr),&m=n,\\[2pt]0,&m\ne n,\end{cases}$$
where $\cdot$ is the pointwise (internal tensor) product of class functions on
$S_m$; extend $*$ bilinearly to all of $\Lambda$. Call $*$ the
**internal (Kronecker) product** of symmetric functions.

**Well-definedness.** For $m=n$ the class functions $\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(f)$
and $\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(g)$ lie in $R(S_m)$, the integral span of the
irreducible characters of $S_m$
([[def-graded-ordinary-representation-ring-of-symmetric-groups]]). The
pointwise product of two honest characters of $S_m$ is again an honest
character, namely the character of the tensor product of the underlying
representations ([[thm-characters-of-direct-sums-tensor-products-and-duals]]),
and products of $\mathbb Z$-combinations of characters are computed
bilinearly; hence the pointwise product of two elements of $R(S_m)$ lies in
$R(S_m)$, and applying the isomorphism $\operatorname{ch}$ lands in $\Lambda^m$.
The product is therefore well defined and takes $\Lambda^m\times\Lambda^m$ to
$\Lambda^m$.

**Basic properties.** The product is bilinear by construction and inherits
commutativity and associativity from the pointwise product of class functions.
It preserves degrees, in the sense that $\Lambda^m*\Lambda^n\subseteq\Lambda^m$
for $m=n$ and is $0$ for $m\ne n$. On $\Lambda^n$ the unit is
$h_n=s_{(n)}=\operatorname{ch}(\text{trivial character of }S_n)$, because the
trivial character is the unit for pointwise multiplication on $R(S_n)$
([[thm-frobenius-characteristic-sends-specht-characters-to-schur-functions]]
identifies $\operatorname{ch}(\chi^{(n)})=s_{(n)}=h_n$). The graded direct sum
$\Lambda$ has **no global unit** for $*$: if $e\in\Lambda$ had finite degree
support and $n$ were a degree with $e_n=0$ while $\Lambda^n\ne0$, then
$(e*h_n)_n=e_n*h_n=0\ne h_n$, so $e*h_n\ne h_n$; a global unit would require
$e_n$ to be a unit of $(\Lambda^n,*)$ for every $n$. In particular the ordinary
product unit $1\in\Lambda^0$ is not a unit for $*$ on the positive degrees.

**Schur expansion.** For partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$, the definition and
the Specht character dictionary $\operatorname{ch}(\chi^\lambda)=s_\lambda$
([[thm-frobenius-characteristic-sends-specht-characters-to-schur-functions]])
give
$$s_\lambda*s_\mu=\operatorname{ch}\bigl(\chi^\lambda\cdot\chi^\mu\bigr)=\operatorname{ch}\Bigl(\sum_{\nu\vdash n}g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)\chi^\nu\Bigr)=\sum_{\nu\vdash n}g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)\,s_\nu,$$
because $\chi^\lambda\chi^\mu$ is the character of
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ and its decomposition has multiplicities
$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$
([[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]).

No form of the Axiom of Choice is used: the transport goes through the
choice-free Frobenius characteristic isomorphism and finite-dimensional
representation theory of finite groups.

For partitions $\rho,\sigma\vdash n$ one has
$$p_\rho*p_\sigma=\delta_{\rho,\sigma}\,z_\rho\,p_\rho,\qquad
z_\rho=\prod_{i\ge1}i^{m_i(\rho)}m_i(\rho)!,$$
where $m_i(\rho)$ is the number of parts of $\rho$ equal to $i$. Consequently
$$s_\lambda*s_\mu=\sum_{\nu\vdash n}g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)\,s_\nu$$
for all $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$. The internal product on $\Lambda^n$ is therefore
diagonal in the power-sum basis, with $z_\rho$ the diagonal scalars, and it has
the integer structure constants $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ in the Schur basis.

For $d\ge0$ and each partition $\lambda\vdash d$, let $m_\lambda\in\Lambda^d$
be the compatible sequence whose rank-$N$ projection is the monomial orbit
sum $m_\lambda(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$ when $\ell(\lambda)\le N$, and is zero
otherwise. Then $\{m_\lambda:\lambda\vdash d\}$ is a $\mathbb Z$-basis of
$\Lambda^d$.
As $\lambda$ ranges over partitions of length at most $n$, the polynomials $m_\lambda$ form an $R$-basis of $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]^{\operatorname{Sym}_n}$.

For a partition $\lambda$ and an integer $N\ge\ell(\lambda)$, pad $\lambda$
with zero parts to length $N$ and set
$\delta_N=(N-1,N-2,\ldots,0)$. Define the alternating polynomial
$$a_{\lambda+\delta_N}(x_1,\ldots,x_N):=\det\bigl(x_i^{\lambda_j+N-j}\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le N},$$
and define $a_{\delta_N}$ by the same formula with $\lambda=\varnothing$.
The finite-rank Schur polynomial is
$$s_\lambda(x_1,\ldots,x_N):=\frac{a_{\lambda+\delta_N}(x_1,\ldots,x_N)}{a_{\delta_N}(x_1,\ldots,x_N)}.$$
For $0\le N<\ell(\lambda)$, define $s_\lambda(x_1,\ldots,x_N):=0$.
Thus a component is specified at every rank, including rank zero; empty
determinants have value $1$.

**Well-definedness and stability.** The exponents $\lambda_j+N-j$ are
strictly decreasing, so the numerator is alternating. Setting $x_i=x_j$
makes it zero; the factor theorem therefore gives divisibility by each
$x_i-x_j$ in $\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_N]$. These pairwise nonassociate prime
factors therefore have product $a_{\delta_N}$ dividing the numerator, so the quotient is an
integral polynomial. Since numerator and denominator both change by the sign
of a variable permutation, their quotient is symmetric. Its degree is
$|\lambda|$.

If $N+1>\ell(\lambda)$, setting $x_{N+1}=0$ in the rank-$(N+1)$ numerator
and denominator expands each determinant along its last row; both resulting
minors have the common factor $x_1\cdots x_N$, and after cancelling it the
quotient is exactly the rank-$N$ quotient. At the remaining boundary
$N+1=\ell(\lambda)>0$, every exponent in the rank-$(N+1)$ numerator
is positive, so its last row becomes zero when $x_{N+1}=0$.
The denominator specializes to
$(x_1\cdots x_N)a_{\delta_N}$, a nonzero polynomial (equal to $1$ when
$N=0$). Specializing the polynomial identity
$a_{\lambda+\delta_{N+1}}=a_{\delta_{N+1}}s_\lambda$
and cancelling this nonzero polynomial shows that the specialized Schur
polynomial is zero, as required by the rank-$N$ definition. Below this
boundary both components are zero. Hence these polynomials form a
compatible sequence in the inverse limit
[[def-stable-graded-ring-of-symmetric-functions]], defining
$s_\lambda\in\Lambda^{|\lambda|}$. With the empty determinant equal to $1$,
$s_{\varnothing}=1$. The partition length and padding convention is that of
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]].

At the minimal rank $N=1$, the one-box partition gives
$s_{(1)}(x_1)=x_1$ directly from the quotient; its stable sequence is
nonzero.

For integers $N,d\ge0$, let $A_N^d$ be the degree-$d$ homogeneous part of
$\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_N]^{S_N}$, using
[[def-symmetric-polynomial]] and the convention $A_0^0=\mathbb Z$ and
$A_0^d=0$ for $d>0$. For $M\ge N$, the transition
$\pi_{M,N}:A_M^d\to A_N^d$ sets $x_{N+1},\ldots,x_M$ equal to zero.
These maps compose, so define
$$\Lambda^d:=\varprojlim_{N\ge0}A_N^d,\qquad \Lambda:=\bigoplus_{d\ge0}\Lambda^d.$$

An element of $\Lambda^d$ is a compatible sequence of homogeneous
degree-$d$ symmetric polynomials, one in each rank. Multiplication of a
degree-$a$ sequence and a degree-$b$ sequence is coordinatewise polynomial
multiplication and lies in $\Lambda^{a+b}$; compatibility follows because
each $\pi_{M,N}$ is a ring homomorphism. Extend this product distributively
to $\Lambda$. The unit is the compatible constant sequence $1$, and each
element of $\Lambda$ has only finitely many nonzero homogeneous components.

This direct sum is not the ungraded inverse limit of the rings
$\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_N]^{S_N}$. For example, the compatible sequence
$\prod_{i=1}^N(1+x_i)$ belongs to that ungraded inverse limit and has nonzero
homogeneous components in every degree, so it is not an element of the direct
sum $\Lambda$. The partition notation and empty partition follow
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]].

Work in $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}:=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda$, the
$\mathbb Q$-scalar extension of the stable graded ring
([[def-stable-graded-ring-of-symmetric-functions]]). Its power sums
$p_1,p_2,\dots$ ([[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]])
are algebraically independent generators:
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q[p_1,p_2,\dots]$, and for every $d$ the products
$p_\lambda$, $\lambda\vdash d$, form a $\mathbb Q$-basis of
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^d$
([[prop-power-sums-form-a-rational-not-integral-stable-basis]]).

A **specialization** is a $\mathbb Q$-algebra homomorphism
$f\mapsto f[A]$ from $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}$ to a commutative
$\mathbb Q$-algebra. By the algebraic independence of the power sums, a
specialization is determined by the sequence of values $\bigl(p_k[A]\bigr)_{k\ge1}$,
and conversely every sequence of elements of a commutative $\mathbb Q$-algebra
extends uniquely to a specialization. For specializations $A,B$, a scalar
$c\in\mathbb Q$ and a one-letter alphabet $t$ one defines the specializations
$A+B$, $-A$, $AB$, $c\cdot A$ and $tA$ by their power-sum values

$$p_k[A+B]:=p_k[A]+p_k[B],\qquad p_k[-A]:=-p_k[A],\qquad p_k[AB]:=p_k[A]\,p_k[B],$$

$$p_k[c\cdot A]:=c\,p_k[A],\qquad p_k[t]:=t^k\ \ \text{and hence}\ \ p_k[tA]=t^k p_k[A].$$

Here $c\cdot A$ is a coefficient multiplicity, to be distinguished from the
one-letter alphabet $t$, for which $p_k[t]=t^k$ is a power and
$p_k[tA]=t^k p_k[A]$; all occurrences of $tX$, $t^{-1}$, $tA$ and
$\sigma[t]$ on this page use this one-letter convention. The symbol $1$
denotes the one-letter alphabet with $p_k[1]=1$ for all $k$, and $-1$ denotes
its plethystic negative with $p_k[-1]=-1$ for all $k$
([[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]]); it is
**not** the ordinary one-letter alphabet whose letter is minus one, for which
$p_k$ would equal $(-1)^k$. One writes $f[A+B]$, $f[-A]$, $f[AB]$ and
$f[c\cdot A]$ for the images of $f$ under these specializations.

Define $X^{\perp}$ to be the specialization with $f[X^{\perp}]:=f^{\perp}$ for
all $f$, where $f^{\perp}$ is the adjoint of multiplication by $f$ with respect
to the Hall inner product $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_H$
([[def-hall-inner-product-on-symmetric-functions]]), characterized by
$\langle f^{\perp}g,h\rangle_H=\langle g,fh\rangle_H$. It exists and is unique
because the Hall form is nondegenerate on each finite-dimensional graded piece
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^d$; the adjoints of commuting multiplication operators
commute, so the operators $f^{\perp}$ span a commutative
$\mathbb Q$-algebra and $X^{\perp}$ is a specialization in the sense above.

Define the series
$$\sigma[X]:=\sum_{n\ge0}h_n[X],$$
$h_n$ the complete homogeneous symmetric function
([[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]]).
Here $\sigma$ is interpreted in the graded completion of $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}$
(or with a formal degree variable): it is a formal series, not an element of
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}$, and every occurrence of $\sigma$ below is to be read
degree by degree. Every Hall pairing of a series with a polynomial is the
finite sum obtained by truncating to the degrees of the polynomial. No
convergence of a scalar infinite sum is asserted, and no value of $\sigma$ at
a specialization with infinitely many letters is interpreted analytically.

Work in $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda$. For a
partition $\rho$ write
$m_i(\rho):=\#\{j:\rho_j=i\}$ and
$z_\rho:=\prod_{i\ge1}i^{m_i(\rho)}m_i(\rho)!$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]]).

For partitions $\lambda$ and $\rho$ of the same integer, let $N(\lambda,\rho)$
be the number of ways to distribute the cycles of a permutation $w$ of cycle
type $\rho$ among the $\ell(\lambda)$ rows, labelled $1,\dots,\ell(\lambda)$,
so that row $j$ receives cycles whose lengths sum to $\lambda_j$. Cycles of
equal length count as **distinct** here, because they are distinct cycles of
$w$; equivalently,

$$N(\lambda,\rho)=\sum_{(m_i^{(j)})}\ \prod_{i\ge1}\frac{m_i(\rho)!}{\prod_j m_i^{(j)}!},$$

the sum over all matrices $(m_i^{(j)})$ of nonnegative integers with
$\sum_j m_i^{(j)}=m_i(\rho)$ for every $i$ and
$\sum_i i\,m_i^{(j)}=\lambda_j$ for every $j$; each summand is the product
over $i$ of the number of ways to assign the $m_i(\rho)$ labelled cycles of
length $i$ to rows with the prescribed multiplicities $m_i^{(j)}$, so
$N(\lambda,\rho)$ is a nonnegative integer. Then

$$h_\lambda=\sum_{\rho\vdash|\lambda|}N(\lambda,\rho)\,\frac{p_\rho}{z_\rho}\qquad\text{in }\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}.$$

In particular $h_d=\sum_{\rho\vdash d}p_\rho/z_\rho$ for every $d\ge0$.

For $k\ge1$, the **$k$-th power-sum symmetric polynomial** is

$$p_k:=x_1^k+\cdots+x_n^k.$$

For $k\ge0$, the **$k$-th complete homogeneous symmetric polynomial** is

$$h_k:=\sum_{a_1+\cdots+a_n=k}x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_n^{a_n}.$$

Thus $h_0=1$, while for $n=0$ one has $h_k=0$ when $k>0$. Both families are fixed by every permutation of the variables.

Put $e_0=1$ and $e_k=0$ for $k>n$. For every $k\ge1$,

$$k e_k=\sum_{i=1}^k(-1)^{i-1}e_{k-i}p_i.$$

In particular, for $k\le n$ this recursively relates $e_k$ to $p_1,\ldots,p_k$, while for $k>n$ it gives

$$p_k-e_1p_{k-1}+\cdots+(-1)^ne_np_{k-n}=0.$$

No division is used, so the identities hold over every commutative ring.

For every commutative ring $R$ and every $n\in\mathbb N$, substitution $T_k\mapsto e_k$ is an $R$-algebra isomorphism

$$R[T_1,\ldots,T_n]\longrightarrow R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]^{\operatorname{Sym}_n}.$$

Equivalently, every symmetric polynomial has a unique expression $Q(e_1,\ldots,e_n)$.

For $r\ge1$, let $p_r\in\Lambda^r$ be the compatible sequence of finite
power-sum polynomials $p_r(x_1,\ldots,x_N)=\sum_{i=1}^N x_i^r$
([[def-stable-graded-ring-of-symmetric-functions]],
[[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]]). For a
partition $\lambda$, set $p_\lambda:=\prod_i p_{\lambda_i}$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Write
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}:=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda$ and
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^d:=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda^d$. Then
$$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q[p_1,p_2,\ldots],$$
and for every $d\ge0$, the family $\{p_\lambda:\lambda\vdash d\}$ is a
$\mathbb Q$-basis of $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^d$. These families are not in
general $\mathbb Z$-bases of $\Lambda^d$: in degree two,
$h_2=\tfrac12(p_{(1,1)}+p_{(2)})$ has nonintegral coordinates in the power-sum
basis.

Extend the Hall form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_H$ on $\Lambda$
$\mathbb Q$-bilinearly to
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}:=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda$. For partitions
$\lambda$ and $\mu$, let
$$z_\lambda:=\prod_{r\ge1}r^{m_r(\lambda)}m_r(\lambda)!,\qquad m_r(\lambda):=\#\{i:\lambda_i=r\}.$$
Then
$$\langle p_\lambda,p_\mu\rangle_H=\delta_{\lambda\mu}z_\lambda.$$
In particular, power sums of unequal degrees are orthogonal.

For every $d\ge0$, the stable Schur functions $\{s_\lambda:\lambda\vdash d\}$
form a $\mathbb Z$-basis of $\Lambda^d$ and are orthonormal for the Hall form:
$$\langle s_\lambda,s_\mu\rangle_H=\delta_{\lambda\mu}$$
for all partitions $\lambda,\mu$.

For a partition $\lambda$ and an integer $N\ge\ell(\lambda)$, pad $\lambda$
with zero parts to length $N$ and set
$\delta_N=(N-1,N-2,\ldots,0)$. Define the alternating polynomial
$$a_{\lambda+\delta_N}(x_1,\ldots,x_N):=\det\bigl(x_i^{\lambda_j+N-j}\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le N},$$
and define $a_{\delta_N}$ by the same formula with $\lambda=\varnothing$.
The finite-rank Schur polynomial is
$$s_\lambda(x_1,\ldots,x_N):=\frac{a_{\lambda+\delta_N}(x_1,\ldots,x_N)}{a_{\delta_N}(x_1,\ldots,x_N)}.$$
For $0\le N<\ell(\lambda)$, define $s_\lambda(x_1,\ldots,x_N):=0$.
Thus a component is specified at every rank, including rank zero; empty
determinants have value $1$.

**Well-definedness and stability.** The exponents $\lambda_j+N-j$ are
strictly decreasing, so the numerator is alternating. Setting $x_i=x_j$
makes it zero; the factor theorem therefore gives divisibility by each
$x_i-x_j$ in $\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_N]$. These pairwise nonassociate prime
factors therefore have product $a_{\delta_N}$ dividing the numerator, so the quotient is an
integral polynomial. Since numerator and denominator both change by the sign
of a variable permutation, their quotient is symmetric. Its degree is
$|\lambda|$.

If $N+1>\ell(\lambda)$, setting $x_{N+1}=0$ in the rank-$(N+1)$ numerator
and denominator expands each determinant along its last row; both resulting

quotient is exactly the rank-$N$ quotient. At the remaining boundary

is positive, so its last row becomes zero when $x_{N+1}=0$.
The denominator specializes to
$(x_1\cdots x_N)a_{\delta_N}$, a nonzero polynomial (equal to $1$ when
$N=0$). Specializing the polynomial identity
$a_{\lambda+\delta_{N+1}}=a_{\delta_{N+1}}s_\lambda$
and cancelling this nonzero polynomial shows that the specialized Schur
polynomial is zero, as required by the rank-$N$ definition. Below this
boundary both components are zero. Hence these polynomials form a
compatible sequence in the inverse limit
[[def-stable-graded-ring-of-symmetric-functions]], defining
$s_\lambda\in\Lambda^{|\lambda|}$. With the empty determinant equal to $1$,
$s_{\varnothing}=1$. The partition length and padding convention is that of
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]].

At the minimal rank $N=1$, the one-box partition gives
$s_{(1)}(x_1)=x_1$ directly from the quotient; its stable sequence is
nonzero.

Let $\Lambda(x)$ and $\Lambda(y)$ be two copies of the graded ring
[[def-stable-graded-ring-of-symmetric-functions]], with degree pieces
$\Lambda^a(x)$ and $\Lambda^b(y)$. Define the **bidegree-completed tensor
product** by
$$\Lambda(x)\widehat\otimes\Lambda(y):=\prod_{a,b\ge0}\bigl(\Lambda^a(x)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda^b(y)\bigr).$$

Addition is componentwise. If $u=(u_{a,b})$ and $v=(v_{a,b})$, their product
has component
$$ (uv)_{a,b}:=\sum_{i=0}^{a}\sum_{j=0}^{b}u_{i,j}v_{a-i,b-j},$$
where multiplication in each tensor factor is the graded multiplication of
$\Lambda$. This is a finite sum for each fixed $(a,b)$, so it defines a
commutative ring; the unit has component $1\otimes1$ at $(0,0)$ and zero
elsewhere.

The **Cauchy kernel** is the element
$$\Omega(x,y):=\prod_{r,s\ge1}(1-x_r y_s)^{-1}$$
interpreted bidegree by bidegree: its degree-$(d,d)$ component is the stable
degree-$d$ coefficient of the finite products, and all components $(a,b)$ with
$a\ne b$ are zero. Thus $\Omega$ belongs to the diagonal bidegrees of this
completion, not to the finite-support graded ring $\Lambda$ itself.

Let $\Omega(x,y)$ be the Cauchy kernel in the bidegree completion
[[def-bidegree-completed-symmetric-function-tensor-product]]. In
$\Lambda(x)\widehat\otimes\Lambda(y)$,
$$\Omega(x,y)=\sum_\lambda h_\lambda(x)m_\lambda(y)=\sum_\lambda s_\lambda(x)s_\lambda(y).$$
In the componentwise rational completion
$$\prod_{a,b\ge0}\bigl(\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^a(x)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^b(y)\bigr),$$
it also has the expansion
$$\Omega(x,y)=\sum_\lambda z_\lambda^{-1}p_\lambda(x)p_\lambda(y),\qquad z_\lambda:=\prod_{r\ge1}r^{m_r(\lambda)}m_r(\lambda)!,\qquad m_r(\lambda):=\#\{i:\lambda_i=r\}.$$
All three sums are by bidegree $(d,d)$; the empty products indexed by

Let $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$ be a partition with $|\alpha|=\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_k$

an integer. Whenever

$$n\;\ge\;|\alpha|+\alpha_1,$$

define the **first-row padding** of $\alpha$ to size $n$ to be
$$\alpha[n]:=\bigl(n-|\alpha|,\ \alpha_1,\ \alpha_2,\ \dots,\ \alpha_k\bigr).$$

The threshold is exact.

**Above the threshold.** Suppose $n\ge|\alpha|+\alpha_1$. Then
$n-|\alpha|\ge\alpha_1\ge0$, so every entry of the displayed sequence is a
nonnegative integer, the entries sum to $(n-|\alpha|)+|\alpha|=n$, and the
sequence is weakly decreasing because $n-|\alpha|\ge\alpha_1$ and $\alpha$ is
weakly decreasing ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).
If $\alpha$ is nonempty then $\alpha_1\ge1$, hence $n-|\alpha|\ge1$ and the
displayed sequence is a partition of $n$ with positive parts. If
$\alpha=\varnothing$ then the displayed sequence is $(n)$; this is a partition
of $n$ for every $n\ge1$, while for $n=0$ one takes $\varnothing[0]:=\varnothing$,
the unique partition of $0$. Thus the padding is defined and is a partition of
$n$ on the whole displayed range.

**Below the threshold.** If $\alpha$ is nonempty and $n<|\alpha|+\alpha_1$,
then $n-|\alpha|<\alpha_1$; if also $n\ge|\alpha|$ the leading entry is
nonnegative but smaller than the second entry $\alpha_1$, and if $n<|\alpha|$
it is negative. In both cases the displayed sequence is not a partition, so
$\alpha[n]$ is left undefined. The threshold $|\alpha|+\alpha_1$ is therefore
the exact size at which the padded family begins: at
$n=|\alpha|+\alpha_1$ the padding equals $(\alpha_1,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\dots)$,
which is a partition with a repeated first part when $\alpha$ is nonempty.

it asserts no constancy of any quantity along the family and no stability
property. The same notation is used by the FI-module and
representation-stability developments, where the padding threshold reappears as
the generation degree of the family under consideration.

**Padded sequences.** For a partition $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$ and an
integer $n$ the first-row padding is the sequence
$\alpha[n]:=(n-|\alpha|,\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$, a partition of $n$ exactly
when $n\ge|\alpha|+\alpha_1$
([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]],
[[def-padded-kronecker-coefficient-sequence]]).

**The Jacobi–Trudi completion.** For an arbitrary finite sequence of integers
$\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_m)$, define
$$s_\mu:=\det\bigl(h_{\mu_j-j+i}\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le m},$$
where $h_0=1$ and $h_k=0$ for $k<0$
([[thm-jacobi-trudi-and-dual-jacobi-trudi-identities]]); for the empty sequence
the empty determinant is $1$. Every such determinant is $0$ or $\pm1$ times a
Schur function. Indeed, put $q_j:=\mu_j+m-j$. If $q_j=q_k$ for $j\ne k$, the
$j$-th and $k$-th columns of the matrix agree, so the determinant vanishes.
Otherwise let $\sigma$ be the permutation sorting $q$ into decreasing order
$q_{\sigma(1)}>\cdots>q_{\sigma(m)}$ and set $\nu_j:=q_{\sigma(j)}+j-m$; then
$\nu$ is weakly decreasing and, permuting columns with sign
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$ and using
$h_{\nu_j-j+i}=h_{q_{\sigma(j)}+i-m}$, the determinant equals
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\det(h_{\nu_j-j+i})$. If $\min_jq_j<0$ then
$\nu_m<0$ and the last column of this determinant is zero, so the value is

negative index and vanishes.

$\Lambda$ ([[def-stable-schur-function-by-bialternants]]), so there are unique
$\mathbb Z$-linear endomorphisms $U_n$ ($n\in\mathbb Z$) and $V$ of $\Lambda$
determined on the Schur basis by
$$U_n(s_\lambda):=s_{\lambda[n]},\qquad V(s_\lambda):=s_{\lambda+(1)},$$
where $\lambda+(1)=(\lambda_1+1,\lambda_2,\dots)$. Thus $U_n$ carries

degree-preserving product of
[[def-internal-product-on-symmetric-functions]] and
[[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]. For partitions
$\alpha,\beta$, define $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$ to be the least
integer $n_0\ge0$ such that

exact value of $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$ are proved in
[[thm-exact-global-stabilization-threshold-for-a-fixed-kronecker-product]].

representations ([[thm-characters-of-direct-sums-tensor-products-and-duals]]),
and products of $\mathbb Z$-combinations of characters are computed
bilinearly; hence the pointwise product of two elements of $R(S_m)$ lies in
$R(S_m)$, and applying the isomorphism $\operatorname{ch}$ lands in $\Lambda^m$.
The product is therefore well defined and takes $\Lambda^m\times\Lambda^m$ to
$\Lambda^m$.

**Basic properties.** The product is bilinear by construction and inherits
commutativity and associativity from the pointwise product of class functions.
It preserves degrees, in the sense that $\Lambda^m*\Lambda^n\subseteq\Lambda^m$
for $m=n$ and is $0$ for $m\ne n$. On $\Lambda^n$ the unit is
$h_n=s_{(n)}=\operatorname{ch}(\text{trivial character of }S_n)$, because the
trivial character is the unit for pointwise multiplication on $R(S_n)$
([[thm-frobenius-characteristic-sends-specht-characters-to-schur-functions]]
identifies $\operatorname{ch}(\chi^{(n)})=s_{(n)}=h_n$). The graded direct sum
$\Lambda$ has **no global unit** for $*$: if $e\in\Lambda$ had finite degree
support and $n$ were a degree with $e_n=0$ while $\Lambda^n\ne0$, then
$(e*h_n)_n=e_n*h_n=0\ne h_n$, so $e*h_n\ne h_n$; a global unit would require
$e_n$ to be a unit of $(\Lambda^n,*)$ for every $n$. In particular the ordinary
product unit $1\in\Lambda^0$ is not a unit for $*$ on the positive degrees.

the Specht character dictionary $\operatorname{ch}(\chi^\lambda)=s_\lambda$
([[thm-frobenius-characteristic-sends-specht-characters-to-schur-functions]])
give
$$s_\lambda*s_\mu=\operatorname{ch}\bigl(\chi^\lambda\cdot\chi^\mu\bigr)=\operatorname{ch}\Bigl(\sum_{\nu\vdash n}g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)\chi^\nu\Bigr)=\sum_{\nu\vdash n}g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)\,s_\nu,$$
because $\chi^\lambda\chi^\mu$ is the character of
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ and its decomposition has multiplicities
$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$
([[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]).

choice-free Frobenius characteristic isomorphism and finite-dimensional
representation theory of finite groups.

Fix an integer $n\ge0$ and work over $\mathbb C$. Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be
partitions of $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]), and let

([[def-tensor-product-of-complex-representations]],
[[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]). The

$\nu\vdash n$ is the multiplicity of $S^\nu$ in this tensor product:

$$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu):=\frac{\dim_{\mathbb C}\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}}{\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu},$$

where $\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}$ is the isotypic
component of type $S^\nu$
([[def-isotypic-component-of-a-completely-reducible-representation]]).

finite-dimensional, and $\operatorname{char}\mathbb C=0$ does not divide the
order of the finite group $S_n$, so complex Maschke's theorem gives complete

([[thm-maschkes-theorem-for-finite-groups-over-fields-whose-characteristic-does-not-divide-the-group-order]],
[[cor-finite-dimensional-representations-are-completely-reducible-when-char-k-does-not-divide-group-order]],

$S^\nu$, $\nu\vdash n$, are a complete list of pairwise inequivalent
irreducible $S_n$-modules
([[thm-complex-specht-modules-are-irreducible]],
[[thm-complex-irreducibles-of-symmetric-groups-are-specht-modules]],
[[cor-distinct-specht-modules-are-inequivalent]]). Consequently a decomposition
into irreducibles has the form
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\cong\bigoplus_{\nu\vdash n}m_\nu S^\nu$
with nonnegative integer multiplicities $m_\nu$, and the isotypic component of
type $S^\nu$ is the direct sum of exactly the $m_\nu$ copies of $S^\nu$
appearing in any such decomposition; in particular

and $\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu>0$ because $S^\nu$ is irreducible. Hence
$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=m_\nu$ is a nonnegative integer, independent of the chosen
decomposition, and $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ is by definition the multiplicity of
$S^\nu$ in $S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$.

**The internal product.** For partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ call
$$(\lambda,\mu)\longmapsto S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$$
the **internal (Kronecker) product** of the $S_n$-representations $S^\lambda$
and $S^\mu$. Unlike the outer induction product
$\operatorname{Ind}_{S_a\times S_b}^{S_{a+b}}(S^\alpha\boxtimes S^\beta)$ of
[[thm-outer-littlewood-richardson-rule]], which takes a pair of modules of
degrees $a$ and $b$ to a module of degree $a+b$, the internal product keeps the
rank: both inputs and the output are $S_n$-modules of the same degree $n$. The
two operations are different constructions on different data; the outer product
is mentioned here only for contrast and is not used in this definition.

the Specht classification and the isotypic decomposition are finite-dimensional

for all partitions $\lambda,\mu$.

For $r\ge1$, let $p_r\in\Lambda^r$ be the compatible sequence of finite

([[def-stable-graded-ring-of-symmetric-functions]],
[[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]]). For a
partition $\lambda$, set $p_\lambda:=\prod_i p_{\lambda_i}$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Write
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}:=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda$ and
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^d:=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda^d$. Then
$$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q[p_1,p_2,\ldots],$$
and for every $d\ge0$, the family $\{p_\lambda:\lambda\vdash d\}$ is a

general $\mathbb Z$-bases of $\Lambda^d$: in degree two,

basis.

derivations.claim: *Internal-product kernel.* For $f,g\in\Lambda^d_{\mathbb Q}$ and all specializations $U,V,W$ one has $\langle f[U]g[V]\,|\,\sigma[UVW]\rangle_{U,V}=(f*g)[W]$. Writing $f=\sum_\rho a_\rho p_\rho$ and $g=\sum_\rho b_\rho p_\rho$, [F5] gives $\langle f[U]g[V],p_\rho[U]p_\rho[V]p_\rho[W]\rangle_{U,V}=a_\rho z_\rho\cdot b_\rho z_\rho\cdot p_\rho[W]$, so the left side is $\sum_{\rho\vdash d}a_\rho b_\rho z_\rho p_\rho[W]=(f*g)[W]$ by [F5].

*The generating function $F(t)=\sum_{n\ge0}(U_ns_\alpha)*(U_ns_\beta)t^n$.* By [F1] and [F3], the degree-$n$ part of $\sigma[A]s_\alpha[A-1]$ is $U_ns_\alpha$, and likewise for $\beta$; the bidegree-$(n,n)$ part of the product $\sigma[A]s_\alpha[A-1]\,\sigma[B]s_\beta[B-1]$ is therefore $(U_ns_\alpha)[A](U_ns_\beta)[B]$. Pairing against $\sigma[tXAB]=\sum_nt^nh_n[XAB]$ and applying step 1.1 in each degree gives $F(t)=\langle\sigma[A]s_\alpha[A-1]\,\sigma[B]s_\beta[B-1]\,|\,\sigma[tXAB]\rangle_{A,B}$, a formula in which the coefficient of $t^n$ is finite by [F1].

*Hall adjunction.* For every specialization $W$ and every $h\in\Lambda$, the adjunction of [F2] with the one-letter alphabet $1$ reads $\sigma[A^{\perp}]h[A]=h[A+1]$; equivalently $\langle\sigma[A]u[A],W[A]\rangle_A=\langle u[A],W[A+1]\rangle_A$ and, in the reverse direction, $\langle u[A-1],W[A]\rangle_A=\langle u[A],\sigma[-A]W[A]\rangle_A$. Applying this in the $A$-variable and then in the $B$-variable to the identity of step 2.1 turns $\sigma[A]\sigma[B]$ into the translation $A\mapsto A+1$, $B\mapsto B+1$ of the kernel and moves the shifts $-1$ of $s_\alpha,s_\beta$ onto the kernel: $F(t)=\langle s_\alpha[A]s_\beta[B]\,|\,\sigma[tX(A+1)(B+1)-A-B]\rangle_{A,B}$.

By [F3], the coefficient of $t^n$ in $\sigma[tX]h[tX-1]$ is $U_nh$ for every finite-degree $h$, and $R_{\alpha,\beta}[tX-1]$ is the specialization of the element $R_{\alpha,\beta}\in\Lambda_Z$ introduced in the statement, so comparing the coefficient of $t^n$ gives $(U_ns_\alpha)*(U_ns_\beta)=U_nR_{\alpha,\beta}$ for every $n\ge0$; for $n<0$ one has $U_n=0$ by [F1], so no negative index is asserted.

*Finiteness of $R$.* Factor the kernel of $R$ as $\sigma[ZAB]\sigma[ZA]\sigma[ZB]\sigma[AB]$. In the $(a,b)$-bidegree of the pairing, the four factors contribute bidegrees $(j,j)$, $(m,0)$, $(0,n)$, $(l,l)$ with $j+m+l=a$ and $j+n+l=b$, so $0\le j,m,n,l\le a+b$ and the $Z$-degree is $j+m+n=b+m-l\le a+b$. No infinite sum of symmetric functions is evaluated.

*The Littlewood expression.* Expand the four factors of the kernel of $R$ with the Cauchy identity and the product-alphabet identity [F2] and [F4]: $\sigma[ZAB]=\sum_{\zeta,\delta,\epsilon}s_\zeta[Z]g^\zeta_{\delta\epsilon}s_\delta[A]s_\epsilon[B]$, $\sigma[ZA]=\sum_\sigma s_\sigma[Z]s_\sigma[A]$, $\sigma[ZB]=\sum_\rho s_\rho[Z]s_\rho[B]$ and $\sigma[AB]=\sum_\tau s_\tau[A]s_\tau[B]$. This is exactly the displayed Littlewood expression, and the sum is finite because $c$- and $g$-coefficients vanish outside the size constraints.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$, let $\lambda$ be a partition with
$m:=|\lambda|$ and first part $\lambda_1$, and put $d:=m+\lambda_1$. For a
partition $\mu\vdash n$ write $V_\mu$ for the irreducible $kS_n$-module with
label $\mu$
([[lem-specht-modules-classify-irreducibles-over-characteristic-zero-fields]]),
and for $n\ge d$ let $\lambda[n]$ be the first-row padding of $\lambda$ to $n$
([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]]).

Then there is a sub-FI-module $V(\lambda)$ of the free FI-module $M(\lambda)$
([[def-free-fi-module-generated-by-an-sm-module]]) with

$$V(\lambda)_n\cong V_{\lambda[n]}\quad(n\ge d),\qquad V(\lambda)_n=0\quad(n<d),$$

so that the value of this FI-module at $[n]$ is the irreducible $kS_n$-module
denoted $V(\lambda)_n$ in [[def-weight-of-a-characteristic-zero-fi-module]].
This FI-module is generated in degree $\le d$
([[def-finite-generation-and-generation-degree-of-an-fi-module]]), and its
generation degree is exactly $d$. It has

$$\operatorname{weight}(V(\lambda))=m,\qquad\operatorname{inj-deg}(V(\lambda))=0,\qquad\operatorname{surj-deg}(V(\lambda))=\operatorname{stab-deg}(V(\lambda))=\lambda_1,$$

where weight is as in [[def-weight-of-a-characteristic-zero-fi-module]] and the
three degrees are as in
[[def-injectivity-surjectivity-and-stability-degree-of-an-fi-module]]. No
choice principle is used.

Let $V$ and $W$ be FI-modules over a commutative ring $k$, with pointwise
tensor product $(V\otimes W)_S:=V_S\otimes_kW_S$ and transition maps
$f_*\otimes f_*$. If $V$ and $W$ are finitely generated, then $V\otimes W$ is
finitely generated; more precisely, if $V$ is generated in degree $\le m_1$
and $W$ in degree $\le m_2$
([[def-finite-generation-and-generation-degree-of-an-fi-module]]), then
$V\otimes W$ is generated in degree $\le m_1+m_2$. No choice principle is
used.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$
with finite-dimensional values
([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]). Then $V$ is finitely generated if and only
if the consistent sequence $(V_n,\varphi_n)$ determined by $V$ is uniformly
representation stable
([[def-uniform-representation-stability-for-consistent-sn-sequences]],
[[def-finite-generation-and-generation-degree-of-an-fi-module]]). No choice
principle is used.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$. A **consistent sequence** is a
sequence $(V_n,\varphi_n)_{n\ge0}$ in which each $V_n$ is a finite-dimensional
left $kS_n$-module and each $\varphi_n\colon V_n\to V_{n+1}$ is
$S_n$-equivariant, the target being regarded as an $S_n$-module by restriction
along the standard inclusion $S_n\hookrightarrow S_{n+1}$ that fixes $n$. An
FI-module $V$ over $k$ with finite-dimensional values
([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]) determines such a sequence by
$V_n:=V([n])$ and $\varphi_n:=f_*$ for the standard inclusions
$f\colon[n]\to[n+1]$; these maps are $S_n$-equivariant by functoriality and the
conjugation action, since $f\circ\sigma=\Phi_f(\sigma)\circ f$ with
$\Phi_f(\sigma)$ the extension of $\sigma$ by the fixed point $n$.

The sequence is **uniformly representation stable with stable range $n\ge N$**
when all three of the following hold.

1. **(I) Injectivity.** The map $\varphi_n\colon V_n\to V_{n+1}$ is injective for
   every $n\ge N$.
2. **(II) Surjectivity.** The $S_{n+1}$-span of the image $\varphi_n(V_n)$ is
   all of $V_{n+1}$ for every $n\ge N$.
3. **(III) Multiplicities.** For each partition $\lambda$ and each $n$ with
   $n\ge|\lambda|+\lambda_1$, let $V(\lambda)_n$ be the irreducible $kS_n$-module
   indexed by the first-row padding $\lambda[n]=(n-|\lambda|,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\dots)$
   ([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]]), namely the scalar extension
   $k\otimes_{\mathbb Q}S^{\lambda[n]}_{\mathbb Q}$ of the rational Specht model,
   which is the unique irreducible $kS_n$-module with that label
   ([[lem-specht-modules-classify-irreducibles-over-characteristic-zero-fields]];
   over $\mathbb C$ this is the published complex Specht classification
   [[thm-complex-specht-modules-are-irreducible]]). Decompose
   $V_n\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda}c_{\lambda,n}V(\lambda)_n$ with multiplicities
   $c_{\lambda,n}\ge0$, the sum over those $\lambda$ with
   $n\ge|\lambda|+\lambda_1$. Then for every fixed $\lambda$ the multiplicity
   $c_{\lambda,n}$ is independent of $n$ for all $n\ge N$.

The sequence is **uniformly representation stable** when it is so for some
$N\ge0$. All three conditions are part of the definition, and (II) is not a
consequence of (I) and (III): the sequence with $V_n=k^2$ carrying the trivial
$S_n$-action and $\varphi_n$ the inclusion of the first coordinate is injective
and has constant multiplicities $c_{\varnothing,n}=2$, but its images span only
a one-dimensional subspace of $V_{n+1}$. No choice principle is used.

([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]), and let

[[cor-finite-dimensional-representations-are-completely-reducible-when-char-k-does-not-divide-group-order]],

**The internal product.** For partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ call
$$(\lambda,\mu)\longmapsto S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$$
the **internal (Kronecker) product** of the $S_n$-representations $S^\lambda$
and $S^\mu$. Unlike the outer induction product
$\operatorname{Ind}_{S_a\times S_b}^{S_{a+b}}(S^\alpha\boxtimes S^\beta)$ of
[[thm-outer-littlewood-richardson-rule]], which takes a pair of modules of

No form of the Axiom of Choice is used: the tensor product, Maschke's theorem,
the Specht classification and the isotypic decomposition are finite-dimensional

Let $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$ be a partition with $|\alpha|=\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_k$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]), and let $n\ge0$ be
an integer. Whenever

$$n\;\ge\;|\alpha|+\alpha_1,$$

define the **first-row padding** of $\alpha$ to size $n$ to be
$$\alpha[n]:=\bigl(n-|\alpha|,\ \alpha_1,\ \alpha_2,\ \dots,\ \alpha_k\bigr).$$

The threshold is exact.

**Above the threshold.** Suppose $n\ge|\alpha|+\alpha_1$. Then
$n-|\alpha|\ge\alpha_1\ge0$, so every entry of the displayed sequence is a
nonnegative integer, the entries sum to $(n-|\alpha|)+|\alpha|=n$, and the
sequence is weakly decreasing because $n-|\alpha|\ge\alpha_1$ and $\alpha$ is
weakly decreasing ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).
If $\alpha$ is nonempty then $\alpha_1\ge1$, hence $n-|\alpha|\ge1$ and the
displayed sequence is a partition of $n$ with positive parts. If
$\alpha=\varnothing$ then the displayed sequence is $(n)$; this is a partition
of $n$ for every $n\ge1$, while for $n=0$ one takes $\varnothing[0]:=\varnothing$,
the unique partition of $0$. Thus the padding is defined and is a partition of
$n$ on the whole displayed range.

**Below the threshold.** If $\alpha$ is nonempty and $n<|\alpha|+\alpha_1$,
then $n-|\alpha|<\alpha_1$; if also $n\ge|\alpha|$ the leading entry is
nonnegative but smaller than the second entry $\alpha_1$, and if $n<|\alpha|$
it is negative. In both cases the displayed sequence is not a partition, so
$\alpha[n]$ is left undefined. The threshold $|\alpha|+\alpha_1$ is therefore
the exact size at which the padded family begins: at
$n=|\alpha|+\alpha_1$ the padding equals $(\alpha_1,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\dots)$,
which is a partition with a repeated first part when $\alpha$ is nonempty.

**Neutrality of the notation.** This definition records a family of partitions;
it asserts no constancy of any quantity along the family and no stability
property. The same notation is used by the FI-module and
representation-stability developments, where the padding threshold reappears as
the generation degree of the family under consideration.

Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $n\ge0$. For every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ the field-valued Specht module $S^\lambda_F$ of
[[def-polytabloid-specht-module-over-an-arbitrary-field]] is nonzero and
irreducible, distinct partitions give non-isomorphic modules, and every
irreducible $FS_n$-module is isomorphic to exactly one of them. Consequently,
by Maschke's theorem, every finite-dimensional $FS_n$-module is a direct sum of
copies of the $S^\lambda_F$; thus the irreducible $FS_n$-modules are indexed by
the partitions of $n$ and the modules $\{S^\lambda_F:\lambda\vdash n\}$ form a
complete irredundant list.

This is the constituent convention used throughout the pair: over
$F=\mathbb C$ it specialises to the published complex classification, and over
a general characteristic-zero field $F$ it is proved by extending the rational
Specht models along $\mathbb Q\to F$, never by a scalar extension from
$\mathbb C$ to $F$.

derivations.claim: By [F1] the assignment $n\mapsto V_{\alpha[n]}$ (and $0$ below the threshold) is a finitely generated FI-module $V(\alpha)$ over $k$ with finite-dimensional values, and likewise $V(\beta)$.

By [F2] the pointwise tensor product $V(\alpha)\otimes V(\beta)$ is a finitely generated FI-module with values $V_{\alpha[n]}\otimes_kV_{\beta[n]}$ at rank $n$; all values are finite dimensional over $k$ because each is a tensor product of finite-dimensional $kS_n$-modules.

By [F3] applied to $V(\alpha)\otimes V(\beta)$ there are an integer $N$ and a finite family of partitions $\lambda$ with multiplicities $c_\lambda\ge0$ such that $(V(\alpha)\otimes V(\beta))_n\cong\bigoplus_\lambda c_\lambda V_{\lambda[n]}$ for every $n\ge N$; let $S:=\{\lambda:c_\lambda\ne0\}$ and put $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}:=c_\gamma$ for $\gamma\in S$ and $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}:=0$ otherwise, so that $\bigoplus_\lambda c_\lambda V_{\lambda[n]}=\bigoplus_{\gamma\in S}\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}V_{\gamma[n]}$ for $n\ge N$.

Put $N_0:=\max\{N,\,|\alpha|+\alpha_1,\,|\beta|+\beta_1,\,\max_{\lambda\in S}(|\lambda|+\lambda_1)\}$, finite because $S$ is finite. For $n\ge N_0$ the equality of step 3.1 holds with every $V_{\gamma[n]}$, $\gamma\in S$, an honest irreducible of $kS_n$; and the rank-$n$ value also decomposes by [F4] as $\bigoplus_\gamma g^{\gamma[n]}_{\alpha[n],\beta[n]}V_{\gamma[n]}$, the sum over all partitions $\gamma$ (finitely many nonzero, and $V_{\gamma[n]}$ an irreducible of $kS_n$ for $n\ge|\gamma|+\gamma_1$). By the nonisomorphism clause of [F4], the two decompositions have the same labels and multiplicities: $g_n(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}$ for every partition $\gamma$ and every $n\ge N_0$, where for $\gamma\notin S$ this says $g_n(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=0$.

The case $\gamma\notin S$ and $n<m(\gamma)$ also gives $g_n(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=0$ by the convention in the statement, so making $N_0$ larger if necessary the equality $g_n(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}$ holds for all $n\ge N_0$ and all partitions $\gamma$; this is eventual constancy with the finite support $S(\alpha,\beta):=S$. The empty partition is included: $V_{\varnothing[n]}$ is the trivial module, the thresholds $|\varnothing|+\varnothing_1=0$ cause no special case, and the argument did not use any bound on $N_0$ sharper than existence.

No choice principle is used: the FI-module suppliers are $\mathbb Z$-linear constructions on finite-dimensional representation categories, the finite family $S$ and its multiplicities come from [F3], and the comparison of irreducibles in step 4.1 is a finite-dimensional decomposition statement over $k$; the statement is asserted for every field of characteristic $0$.

For partitions $\alpha,\beta$ put $a=|\alpha|$, $b=|\beta|$ and define
$$R_{\alpha,\beta}[Z]:=\langle s_\alpha[A]s_\beta[B]\,|\,\sigma[ZAB+ZA+ZB+AB]\rangle_{A,B},$$
the Hall pairing in the alphabet variables $A,B$
([[def-hall-inner-product-on-symmetric-functions]],
[[def-lambda-ring-specializations-and-the-sigma-series]]).

1. $R_{\alpha,\beta}$ is a finite symmetric-function polynomial in $Z$ of
   degree at most $a+b$.
2. For every integer $n\ge0$,
   $$(U_ns_\alpha)*(U_ns_\beta)=U_nR_{\alpha,\beta},$$
   where $U_n$ is the Jacobi–Trudi completion and $*$ the internal product
   ([[def-first-row-padding-completion-and-the-stabilization-operator]],
   [[def-internal-product-on-symmetric-functions]]); this holds for every
   $n\ge0$, including those $n$ for which the padded sequences $\alpha[n]$,
   $\beta[n]$ are not partitions. Equivalently, with $t$ a one-letter formal
   alphabet,
   $$\sum_{n\ge0}(U_ns_\alpha)*(U_ns_\beta)\,t^n
   =\sigma[tX]\,R_{\alpha,\beta}[tX-1].$$
3. The same polynomial is the finite Littlewood expression
   $$R_{\alpha,\beta}=\sum_{\delta,\epsilon,\tau}
   \bigl((s_\delta s_\tau)^{\perp}s_\alpha\bigr)
   \bigl((s_\epsilon s_\tau)^{\perp}s_\beta\bigr)
   \bigl(s_\delta*s_\epsilon\bigr),$$
   the sum over all triples of partitions, all factors evaluated at $Z$.

Fix partitions $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ and work over a field $k$ of
characteristic $0$, with $V_\lambda$ denoting the irreducible $kS_n$-module
of shape $\lambda\vdash n$
([[lem-specht-modules-classify-irreducibles-over-characteristic-zero-fields]]).
Put $m(\gamma):=\max\{|\alpha|+\alpha_1,\,|\beta|+\beta_1,\,|\gamma|+\gamma_1\}$
and, for $n\ge m(\gamma)$, let
$$g_n(\alpha,\beta,\gamma):=g^{\gamma[n]}_{\alpha[n],\beta[n]}$$
be the multiplicity of $V_{\gamma[n]}$ in
$V_{\alpha[n]}\otimes V_{\beta[n]}$
([[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]],
[[def-padded-kronecker-coefficient-sequence]]); set
$g_n(\alpha,\beta,\gamma):=0$ for $n<m(\gamma)$, where the padded sequences
are not partitions.

Then the sequence $n\mapsto g_n(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ is eventually constant.
More precisely, there is a finite set $S(\alpha,\beta)$ of partitions and
nonnegative integers $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}$ for $\gamma\in S(\alpha,\beta)$,
with $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}:=0$ for $\gamma\notin S(\alpha,\beta)$, such
that $g_n(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}$ for all
sufficiently large $n$ and every partition $\gamma$. No explicit bound on the
stable rank is asserted here; the sharp global bound is a separate claim.

For partitions $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ define the **reduced (stable) Kronecker
coefficient** $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}$ to be the eventual value of the
padded sequence $n\mapsto g_n(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ furnished by
[[thm-murnaghan-stability-for-kronecker-coefficients]]; equivalently
$$\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}:=\lim_{n\to\infty}g^{\gamma[n]}_{\alpha[n],\beta[n]},$$
where the sequence is defined for
$n\ge\max\{|\alpha|+\alpha_1,|\beta|+\beta_1,|\gamma|+\gamma_1\}$ and set to
$0$ below ([[def-padded-kronecker-coefficient-sequence]],
[[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]).

**Well-definedness.** The sequence is eventually constant by the Murnaghan
stability theorem, and the eventual value of an eventually constant sequence
of nonnegative integers is a unique nonnegative integer; no choice is
involved. Two immediate conventions: (i) $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}=
\bar g^\gamma_{\beta,\alpha}$ for all $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$, because
$V_\mu\otimes V_\nu\cong V_\nu\otimes V_\mu$ and the Kronecker coefficients
are symmetric in their two lower indices; (ii) for fixed $\alpha,\beta$ only
finitely many $\gamma$ have $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}\ne0$, because the
finite set $S(\alpha,\beta)$ of the stability theorem carries the whole
support. The values used later and verified in the source's introduction for
$\alpha=\beta=(2)$ are $\bar g^{(2)}_{(2),(2)}=2$ and
$\bar g^{(4)}_{(2),(2)}=1$; they are read off from the displayed stable row
and are not used as logical inputs anywhere on this page.

Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be partitions
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]) and put
$$n_0:=\max\bigl\{|\alpha|+\alpha_1,\ |\beta|+\beta_1,\ |\gamma|+\gamma_1\bigr\},$$
where the first part of the empty partition is read as $0$. For every integer
$n\ge n_0$ the three first-row paddings $\alpha[n]$, $\beta[n]$, $\gamma[n]$ are
partitions of $n$, by
[[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]] and the choice of $n_0$ as the maximum
of the three thresholds. On that range define the **padded Kronecker
coefficient sequence** by
$$g_n(\alpha,\beta,\gamma):=g\bigl(\alpha[n],\ \beta[n],\ \gamma[n]\bigr),$$
the Kronecker coefficient of three partitions of $n$
([[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]).

**Domain.** The threshold $n_0$ is exactly where the common domain of the three
padded families starts: for $n\ge n_0$ all three padded sequences are
partitions of $n$, while for $n<n_0$ at least one of the three padded
sequences is not a partition of $n$ and the expression is left undefined. In
particular the sequence is indexed by the integers $n\ge n_0$ and not by all
$n$.

**No constancy is asserted.** This definition introduces notation only. It
asserts neither that $g_n(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ is eventually constant, nor any
bound on it, nor any comparison between different values of $n$; Murnaghan
stability is a theorem about this sequence proved elsewhere, and this
definition is available as its noncircular input.

Let $\sigma[X]=\sum_{n\ge0}h_n[X]$ be the series of
[[def-lambda-ring-specializations-and-the-sigma-series]], and let
$\langle\ ,\ \rangle_H$ be the Hall form
([[def-hall-inner-product-on-symmetric-functions]]).

1. $\sigma[X]=\prod_{x\in X}(1-x)^{-1}$ and
   $\sigma[-X]=\prod_{x\in X}(1-x)$ for honest alphabets $X$; in particular
   $\sigma[t]=(1-t)^{-1}$ and $\sigma[-t]=1-t$ for the one-letter alphabet
   $t$, as formal series in $t$.
2. $\sigma[A+B]=\sigma[A]\,\sigma[B]$ for all specializations $A,B$, and for
   the one-letter alphabet $t$ one has $\sigma[tA]=\sum_{n\ge0}t^nh_n[A]$.
3. Cauchy identity: $\sigma[XY]=\sum_\lambda s_\lambda[X]s_\lambda[Y]
   =\sum_\lambda z_\lambda^{-1}p_\lambda[X]p_\lambda[Y]$ for all
   specializations $X,Y$, summed by degree.
4. For every specialization $A$, the operator $\sigma[AX^{\perp}]$ is the
   adjoint of multiplication by $\sigma[AX]$:
   $\sigma[AX^{\perp}]f[X]=f[X+A]$ for all $f\in\Lambda$.
5. Reproducing kernel:
   $\langle\sigma[AX]\,|\,f[X]\rangle_X=f[A]$ for all $f\in\Lambda$ and all
   specializations $A$.

**Padded sequences.** For a partition $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$ and an
integer $n$ the first-row padding is the sequence
$\alpha[n]:=(n-|\alpha|,\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$, a partition of $n$ exactly
when $n\ge|\alpha|+\alpha_1$
([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]],
[[def-padded-kronecker-coefficient-sequence]]).

**The Jacobi–Trudi completion.** For an arbitrary finite sequence of integers
$\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_m)$, define
$$s_\mu:=\det\bigl(h_{\mu_j-j+i}\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le m},$$
where $h_0=1$ and $h_k=0$ for $k<0$
([[thm-jacobi-trudi-and-dual-jacobi-trudi-identities]]); for the empty sequence
the empty determinant is $1$. Every such determinant is $0$ or $\pm1$ times a
Schur function. Indeed, put $q_j:=\mu_j+m-j$. If $q_j=q_k$ for $j\ne k$, the
$j$-th and $k$-th columns of the matrix agree, so the determinant vanishes.
Otherwise let $\sigma$ be the permutation sorting $q$ into decreasing order
$q_{\sigma(1)}>\cdots>q_{\sigma(m)}$ and set $\nu_j:=q_{\sigma(j)}+j-m$; then
$\nu$ is weakly decreasing and, permuting columns with sign
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$ and using
$h_{\nu_j-j+i}=h_{q_{\sigma(j)}+i-m}$, the determinant equals
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\det(h_{\nu_j-j+i})$. If $\min_jq_j<0$ then
$\nu_m<0$ and the last column of this determinant is zero, so the value is
$0$; if $\min_jq_j\ge0$ then $\nu$ is a partition of $|\mu|$ with at most $m$
parts and the Jacobi–Trudi identity gives the value
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)s_\nu$. In particular $s_{\alpha[n]}\in\Lambda^n$
for every $n\ge0$, and $s_{\alpha[n]}=0$ for $n<0$: every term of the
determinant expansion has total degree $n$, so for $n<0$ some factor has
negative index and vanishes.

**The operators $U_n$ and $V$.** The Schur functions form a $\mathbb Z$-basis of
$\Lambda$ ([[def-stable-schur-function-by-bialternants]]), so there are unique
$\mathbb Z$-linear endomorphisms $U_n$ ($n\in\mathbb Z$) and $V$ of $\Lambda$
determined on the Schur basis by
$$U_n(s_\lambda):=s_{\lambda[n]},\qquad V(s_\lambda):=s_{\lambda+(1)},$$
where $\lambda+(1)=(\lambda_1+1,\lambda_2,\dots)$. Thus $U_n$ carries
$\Lambda^{|\lambda|}$ into the line spanned by $s_{\lambda[n]}\in\Lambda^n$
(and is the zero map for $n<0$), while $V$ raises degree by one. The operators
are extended linearly, and $V^k$ denotes the $k$-fold iterate of $V$.

**The stabilization index.** The internal product $*$ on $\Lambda$ is the
degree-preserving product of
[[def-internal-product-on-symmetric-functions]] and
[[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]. For partitions
$\alpha,\beta$, define $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$ to be the least
integer $n_0\ge0$ such that
$$s_{\alpha[n_0+k]}*s_{\beta[n_0+k]}=V^k\bigl(s_{\alpha[n_0]}*s_{\beta[n_0]}\bigr)
\qquad\text{for all }k>0,$$
following the source. This definition records the source's convention only: it
does not assert that such an $n_0$ exists, nor that a value of $n_0$ satisfying
the display is least for any other property. Existence, least-ness and the
exact value of $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$ are proved in
[[thm-exact-global-stabilization-threshold-for-a-fixed-kronecker-product]].

Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be partitions
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]) and put
$$n_0:=\max\bigl\{|\alpha|+\alpha_1,\ |\beta|+\beta_1,\ |\gamma|+\gamma_1\bigr\},$$
where the first part of the empty partition is read as $0$. For every integer
$n\ge n_0$ the three first-row paddings $\alpha[n]$, $\beta[n]$, $\gamma[n]$ are
partitions of $n$, by
[[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]] and the choice of $n_0$ as the maximum
of the three thresholds. On that range define the **padded Kronecker
coefficient sequence** by
$$g_n(\alpha,\beta,\gamma):=g\bigl(\alpha[n],\ \beta[n],\ \gamma[n]\bigr),$$
the Kronecker coefficient of three partitions of $n$
([[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]).

**Domain.** The threshold $n_0$ is exactly where the common domain of the three
padded families starts: for $n\ge n_0$ all three padded sequences are
partitions of $n$, while for $n<n_0$ at least one of the three padded
sequences is not a partition of $n$ and the expression is left undefined. In
particular the sequence is indexed by the integers $n\ge n_0$ and not by all
$n$.

**No constancy is asserted.** This definition introduces notation only. It
asserts neither that $g_n(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ is eventually constant, nor any
bound on it, nor any comparison between different values of $n$; Murnaghan
stability is a theorem about this sequence proved elsewhere, and this
definition is available as its noncircular input.

Fix an integer $n\ge0$ and work over $\mathbb C$. Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be
partitions of $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]), and let
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ be the tensor product of their complex
Specht modules, a finite-dimensional complex $S_n$-module
([[def-tensor-product-of-complex-representations]],
[[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]). The
**Kronecker coefficient** $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ of a third partition
$\nu\vdash n$ is the multiplicity of $S^\nu$ in this tensor product:

$$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu):=\frac{\dim_{\mathbb C}\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}}{\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu},$$

where $\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}$ is the isotypic
component of type $S^\nu$
([[def-isotypic-component-of-a-completely-reducible-representation]]).

**Well-definedness.** The module $S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ is
finite-dimensional, and $\operatorname{char}\mathbb C=0$ does not divide the
order of the finite group $S_n$, so complex Maschke's theorem gives complete
reducibility
([[thm-maschkes-theorem-for-finite-groups-over-fields-whose-characteristic-does-not-divide-the-group-order]],
[[cor-finite-dimensional-representations-are-completely-reducible-when-char-k-does-not-divide-group-order]],
[[def-completely-reducible-representation]]). The complex Specht modules
$S^\nu$, $\nu\vdash n$, are a complete list of pairwise inequivalent
irreducible $S_n$-modules
([[thm-complex-specht-modules-are-irreducible]],
[[thm-complex-irreducibles-of-symmetric-groups-are-specht-modules]],
[[cor-distinct-specht-modules-are-inequivalent]]). Consequently a decomposition
into irreducibles has the form
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\cong\bigoplus_{\nu\vdash n}m_\nu S^\nu$
with nonnegative integer multiplicities $m_\nu$, and the isotypic component of
type $S^\nu$ is the direct sum of exactly the $m_\nu$ copies of $S^\nu$
appearing in any such decomposition; in particular
$\dim_{\mathbb C}(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu)_{(S^\nu)}=m_\nu\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu$
and $\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu>0$ because $S^\nu$ is irreducible. Hence
$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=m_\nu$ is a nonnegative integer, independent of the chosen
decomposition, and $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ is by definition the multiplicity of
$S^\nu$ in $S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$.

**The internal product.** For partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ call
$$(\lambda,\mu)\longmapsto S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$$
the **internal (Kronecker) product** of the $S_n$-representations $S^\lambda$
and $S^\mu$. Unlike the outer induction product
$\operatorname{Ind}_{S_a\times S_b}^{S_{a+b}}(S^\alpha\boxtimes S^\beta)$ of
[[thm-outer-littlewood-richardson-rule]], which takes a pair of modules of
degrees $a$ and $b$ to a module of degree $a+b$, the internal product keeps the
rank: both inputs and the output are $S_n$-modules of the same degree $n$. The
two operations are different constructions on different data; the outer product
is mentioned here only for contrast and is not used in this definition.

No form of the Axiom of Choice is used: the tensor product, Maschke's theorem,
the Specht classification and the isotypic decomposition are finite-dimensional
complex representation theory of a finite group.

derivations.claim: *The polynomial $R$ and its Schur coefficients.* By [F1], $R_{\alpha,\beta}$ is a finite element of $\Lambda_Z$ of degree at most $a+b$, so it has a unique finite Schur expansion $R_{\alpha,\beta}=\sum_\gamma r_\gamma s_\gamma$ with $r_\gamma=\langle R_{\alpha,\beta},s_\gamma\rangle_Z$.

*Identification of the coefficients.* Choose $n$ large enough that (i) $n\ge|\alpha|+\alpha_1$ and $n\ge|\beta|+\beta_1$, (ii) $n\ge|\lambda|+\lambda_1$ for every $\lambda$ occurring in the finite support of $R_{\alpha,\beta}$ and for every $\gamma$ in the finite support $S(\alpha,\beta)$ of the reduced coefficients, and (iii) $n$ is at least the Murnaghan stability threshold of [F2]; this is possible by [F1] and [F2]. By [F1], [F4] and the definition of $U_n$, $(U_ns_\alpha)*(U_ns_\beta)=\sigma[tX]R[tX-1]$-coefficient at $t^n$, which is $\sum_\gamma r_\gamma s_{\gamma[n]}$, a sum over honest Schur functions by (ii) with pairwise distinct labels; by [F2] and [F5], the same element is $s_{\alpha[n]}*s_{\beta[n]}=\sum_\gamma\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}s_{\gamma[n]}$, again over honest Schur functions, with the same set of labels by (ii). Comparing the two expansions in the Schur basis of $\Lambda^n$ gives $r_\gamma=\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}$ for every $\gamma$, treating $\gamma$ outside both finite supports as zero on each side.

*First form.* Factor the kernel of $R_{\alpha,\beta}$ as $\sigma[AB]\,\sigma[Z(AB+A+B)]$ and expand the second factor with the Cauchy identity [F3]: $\sigma[Z(AB+A+B)]=\sum_\gamma s_\gamma[Z]s_\gamma[AB+A+B]$. Reading off the coefficient of $s_\gamma[Z]$ in $R_{\alpha,\beta}$ gives $r_\gamma=\langle s_\alpha[A]s_\beta[B]\,|\,\sigma[AB]\,s_\gamma[AB+A+B]\rangle_{A,B}$; combining with step 2.1 yields the displayed Brion formula after renaming the pairing variables $A,B$ to $X,Y$.

*Three-alphabet form.* Sum the first form against $s_\alpha[X]s_\beta[Y]s_\gamma[Z]$ and use the reproducing kernel [F3] twice: for fixed $\gamma$, $\sum_{\alpha,\beta}s_\alpha[X]s_\beta[Y]\langle s_\alpha[A]s_\beta[B],\sigma[AB]s_\gamma[AB+A+B]\rangle_{A,B}=\langle\sigma[XA]\sigma[YB],\sigma[AB]s_\gamma[AB+A+B]\rangle_{A,B}=\sigma[XY]s_\gamma[XY+X+Y]$, where the last equality applies $\langle\sigma[AX]|h[X]\rangle_X=h[A]$ in each variable. Hence $\sum_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}s_\alpha[X]s_\beta[Y]s_\gamma[Z]=\sigma[XY]\sum_\gamma s_\gamma[Z]s_\gamma[XY+X+Y]=\sigma[XY]\sigma[Z(XY+X+Y)]$ by [F3], and $XY+Z(XY+X+Y)=XYZ+XY+XZ+YZ$.

*Finiteness and choice.* In step 2.1 the set of labels is finite by [F1] and [F2]; in step 4.1 each total degree receives finitely many triples with nonzero coefficient, because $\bar g$ vanishes outside the finite support and the Schur expansions are homogeneous. The argument uses no choice principle: the comparably large rank $n$ is a single existential instantiation, and the expansions are finite.

For all partitions $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$,
$$\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}
=\bigl\langle s_\alpha[X]s_\beta[Y]\,\big|\,\sigma[XY]\,s_\gamma[XY+X+Y]\bigr\rangle_{X,Y},$$
the inner product being the Hall inner product extended to symmetric functions
in the two alphabet variables $X,Y$, and $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}$ the
reduced Kronecker coefficient
([[def-reduced-kronecker-coefficient]]).

Equivalently, introducing a third alphabet $Z$,
$$\sum_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}\,
s_\alpha[X]s_\beta[Y]s_\gamma[Z]
=\sigma[XYZ+XY+XZ+YZ],$$
the symmetric Cauchy-type identity for the reduced coefficients, summed over
all triples of partitions and by total degree. Equivalently again, in the
notation of
[[lem-padding-completion-is-compatible-with-the-internal-product]],
$$R_{\alpha,\beta}=\sum_\gamma \bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}\,s_\gamma,$$
the finite Schur expansion of the polynomial $R_{\alpha,\beta}$.

Let $A,B$ be specializations
([[def-lambda-ring-specializations-and-the-sigma-series]]).

- **(a)** For every partition $\lambda$,
  $$s_\lambda[A+B]=\sum_{\mu,\nu}c^\lambda_{\mu,\nu}\,s_\mu[A]\,s_\nu[B],$$
  the sum over pairs of partitions with $|\mu|+|\nu|=|\lambda|$, where
  $c^\lambda_{\mu,\nu}$ is the Littlewood–Richardson coefficient

- **(b)** For every partition $\lambda$,

reduced Kronecker coefficient
([[def-reduced-kronecker-coefficient]]).

s_\alpha[X]s_\beta[Y]s_\gamma[Z]

the symmetric Cauchy-type identity for the reduced coefficients, summed over
all triples of partitions and by total degree. Equivalently again, in the
notation of
[[lem-padding-completion-is-compatible-with-the-internal-product]],
$$R_{\alpha,\beta}=\sum_\gamma \bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}\,s_\gamma,$$
the finite Schur expansion of the polynomial $R_{\alpha,\beta}$.

coefficient** $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}$ to be the eventual value of the
padded sequence $n\mapsto g_n(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ furnished by
[[thm-murnaghan-stability-for-kronecker-coefficients]]; equivalently
$$\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}:=\lim_{n\to\infty}g^{\gamma[n]}_{\alpha[n],\beta[n]},$$
where the sequence is defined for
$n\ge\max\{|\alpha|+\alpha_1,|\beta|+\beta_1,|\gamma|+\gamma_1\}$ and set to
$0$ below ([[def-padded-kronecker-coefficient-sequence]],
[[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]).
